case_data.title: People's AI Stewardship Summits
case_data.provide-a-brief-description-of-the-proje:
A series of 5 one-day public dialogue events bringing together members of the public with experts, innovators, entrepreneurs and other stakeholders to explore hopes, fears and expectations of AI to enable positive change and improve people's lives. The events were led by the Royal Academy of Engineering held in partnership with, and co-hosted by, the Academy's Regional Enterprise Hubs (in Belfast, Glasgow, Liverpool, Swansea and London) to create a unique space for stakeholders to listen to local members of the communities in which they are based.

The rapid proliferation of Generative AI technologies over the past few years, and the breadth of their penetration into areas of public and private life and society, has pushed the questions of safe and responsible development of AI technologies to the fore. But how do members of the public feel about the implications of the huge changes that AI may bring into work, health, finance, transportation and many other key areas of modern day life? What are their hopes and fears for these new tools? And how do they perceive responsibility, safety, and trustworthiness?

This series of summits brought together diverse voices and expertise to consider a wide range of views and to attempt to ensure that the voices of those who will be affected by technological change are listened to and heard by those developing, implementing and overseeing such technological innovations.

What did we hear?
The insights from the summits have informed the Academy's policy advice, enabling consideration of public perspectives alongside those of experts. 

The key five insights are:

1\. Deliberating future of AI: Both stakeholders and members of the public want to have more opportunities for dialogue to hear diverse perspectives and have informed discussions on AI.

2\. Environmental impacts: People want more considerations for the longer-term impacts of AI such as water scarcity and existing infrastructures.

3\. Human oversight and connection: One of the biggest fears was AI hindering or even replacing human connection, especially for vulnerable groups. The need for more human oversight throughout AI development was emphasised strongly.

4\. Regulation: Robust regulations on local, national, and international levels for safe and responsible AI systems. 
   
5\. AI must benefit everyone: AI should be used to actively reduce inequalities and not do more harm those who are already marginalised.
case_data.what-limitations-to-the-project-should-b:
For each summit 30 members of the public were recruited, aiming to create a genuine diversity of lived experiences within the room, whilst acknowledging that such a small sample could not be accurately representative of local demographics. 

What made these summits unique?

• Place-based approach: Local AI experts, policymakers and innovators were able to hear from members of the public directly in which they are based. Discussions surfaced local contexts, needs, and strengths in technological innovation, providing clarity on how they could be leveraged to promote impact-driven entrepreneurship in the long term.

• Inclusive: Diversity of views, quality of conversations, and interaction between public participants and stakeholders provided valuable insights on topics in relation to AI including health, work and skills, education and transport.

• Deliberative: Going beyond simple opinion sampling, the summits created a deliberative space for all participants that enabled mutual listening and the sharing of both expertise and lived experience.

• Positive futures: the summits not only enabled people to express their fears and concerns but challenged them to deliberate together to articulate positive visions for AI that could be societally beneficial, safe and responsible.

2. Environmental impacts: People want more considerations for the longer-term impacts of AI such as water scarcity and existing infrastructures.

“I felt respected when speaking my views and listened to by stakeholders. I felt my voice and opinion mattered.” (Public participant, Liverpool)

“It has been truly inspiring to hear different voices, thoughts, concerns, and ideas about AI and how it may shape the future of healthcare. The event has demonstrated the value of co-creation and ideation.” (Participant- AI Expert in Healthcare, London)

“For the first time, I have experienced the raw fears (and some hope) of the public regarding the development of AI in the context of deception. As an academic/researcher, I have only gained access to these hopes and fears through data analysis. I think the 'human' side of the human-AI interaction had really popped up during the summit.” (Participant- AI expert, London)
case_data.inclusion-efforts:
We worked with a professional recruitment agency, Fieldmouse Research Ltd, to recruit members of the public local to the 5 locations the summits were held in. Fieldmouse were able to recruit participants from a wide range of demographics for each place, including a mix of urban, suburban and rural residents.

Stakeholders were recruited directly by the Academy team from our network of connections and partners across the UK.
case_data.why-is-this-project-important-to-include:
These summits brought 148 members of the public (recruited from a diverse range of socio-economic and cultural backgrounds) together with 90 AI sector stakeholders (innovators, entrepreneurs, researchers, policymakers and civil society practitioners) across 5 locations in Northern Ireland, Scotland, England and Wales. It focuses on exploring people's hopes, fears and expectations for safe and responsible AI -- where and how it could and should bring benefit for everyone, not just a few.

Starting in March 2024 and concluding in July 2025, the series witnessed the growing public awareness of AI, as LLMs took off, from passing awareness to a near universal experience of some level of use. It provided an open and dynamic space for experts and non-experts to discuss and explore what AI could bring to their communities and localities, both benefits and drawbacks. People were able to debate what kinds of benefits should be retained locally from AI innovation as well as at a more national and societal levels.

After each summit a visual and narrative summary was published which captured the flow of the day's discussions in an accessible format -- presenting ideas and issues in a way that almost everyone can understand and appreciate. 25 vox pop videos were also published capturing the thoughts, perceptions and reflections of many of the participants in each location. Together they represent an extraordinary resource of what different people in different parts of the UK thought and felt about AI during that specific time window.

What made these summits unique?

• Place-based approach: Local AI experts, policymakers and innovators were able to hear from members of the public directly in which they are based. Discussions surfaced local contexts, needs, and strengths in technological innovation, providing clarity on how they could be leveraged to promote impact-driven entrepreneurship in the long term.

• Inclusive: Diversity of views, quality of conversations, and interaction between public participants and stakeholders provided valuable insights on topics in relation to AI including health, work and skills, education and transport.

• Deliberative: Going beyond simple opinion sampling, the summits created a deliberative space for all participants that enabled mutual listening and the sharing of both expertise and lived experience.

• Positive futures: the summits not only enabled people to express their fears and concerns but challenged them to deliberate together to articulate positive visions for AI that could be societally beneficial, safe and responsible.
